Today I want to look at one Latin phrase that sits at the center of the common law: stare decisis. It means, more or less, to stand by things decided. When a higher court has decided a legal question, lower courts are expected to decide the same question in the same way. Why does this matter so much? Mainly because of predictability. If similar cases are decided in similar ways, people and companies can plan. A business that signs a contract can predict how a court is likely to read it. But precedent is not a prison. A court can depart from its own earlier decisions, although it does so rarely and with care. The most famous example in the United States is Brown versus Board of Education, in 1954. In that case, the Supreme Court rejected the idea of separate but equal, which it had accepted in Plessy versus Ferguson almost sixty years earlier. So the system is stable, but it is not frozen.

When I applied for my master's degree in the United States, I had to take the TOEFL, and my first practice test was a disaster. I read the first passage the way I read a contract: every word, slowly, twice. By the third passage, I had run out of time. A friend who had taken the test told me to change my method completely. Now I skim the passage first, and I read the first sentence of each paragraph with special care, because that is usually where the main idea is. Then I go to the questions, and I scan the text for the answer to each one. With multiple choice, I try to rule out the wrong options before I choose the right one. The trick is that the correct answer is almost never verbatim. It is a paraphrase of the text. The wrong options often use the exact words of the passage, and that is what makes them dangerous.

First, Pedro skims the whole passage to get the general idea. Then he reads the topic sentence of each paragraph with special care. Next, he reads the first question and scans the text for the answer. After that, he rules out the options that cannot be right. Finally, he chooses the option that paraphrases the text, not the one that repeats it word for word.
